supplement.where: Appendix A in this PDF, pp. 26-31.
supplement.holds: Full pre-course and post-course questionnaire instruments and item wording (Tables A1-A2, pp. 26-28), plus item-level post-course Likert response distributions for flipped learning, the AI agent, and the overall learning setting (Figs. A1-A3, pp. 29-31).

paper_design_summary: Third-year undergraduates in a knit yarn design studio course at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University were compared across two course offerings: a historical control cohort from the previous year (n = 12) and an intervention cohort from the current year (n = 16). The intervention cohort used a cross-device flipped-learning platform with pre-class videos, readiness checks, a curated gallery, and a GenAI image-generation ideation module. The same instructor scored both cohorts with the same rubric (creativity thinking, design skills, problem solving, presentation, attendance, and a weighted total).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not assigned: cohorts are two consecutive course offerings. The current-year cohort received a bundle of a flipped-learning platform (pre-class videos, readiness checks, curated gallery) plus a GenAI image-generation ideation module; the previous-year cohort followed the earlier course version (slide preview before class).
assignment.quote: Because students were not randomly assigned to cohorts and the comparison was made across two academic years, the design cannot fully rule out cohort differences or other contextual factors.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 3.1 Study design (also p. 9, Section 3.1: 'quasi-experimental historical-cohort design')

arms.name: Historical control cohort
arms.description: Previous-year course offering; pre-class preparation by previewing slide materials; no platform and no GenAI module.

arms.name: Intervention cohort
arms.description: Current-year course offering; flipped-learning cross-device platform (micro-videos, readiness checks, gallery) plus GenAI-assisted visual ideation module.

participants.who: Third-year undergraduate students in the same knit yarn design course, taught by the same instructor, at the School of Fashion and Textiles, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; 12 in the previous-year cohort and 16 in the current-year cohort.
participants.quote: The historical control cohort was the previous-year offering of the course (n = 12), and the intervention cohort was the current-year offering (n = 16).
participants.locator: p. 9, Section 3.1 Study design; also p. 13, Section 4.1 and p. 1, Abstract

ai_tool.name_model: A commercial image generation model accessed through an API (footnote 1 links to seed.bytedance.com/zh/seedream4_5); module labeled 'AI Agent' in the platform
ai_tool.how_used: Parameter-guided prompt scaffolding (color, yarn type, stitch structure, texture, material effect, visual style) with optional one to three reference images; students generated, compared, and downloaded images as early-stage visual references. The paper states GenAI was used to support ideation, not to produce final assessed artifacts (pp. 3, 7-8).

task.description: Knit yarn and knitted fabric design project in a studio course: ideation, physical sampling, design development, portfolio and final presentation; both cohorts followed the same project brief and deliverables.
task.duration: One course offering: four lecture sessions followed by nine studio sessions (p. 5)

outcomes.measure_detail: Instructor-scored rubric dimension for produced design work, on a 0-100 scale with weight 20 percent. The same instructor and rubric were used for both cohorts (p. 4, Introduction; p. 9, Fig. 6; p. 10, Section 3.2 and Table 1; p. 11, Section 3.4). The Mann-Whitney U test is a sensitivity analysis of this same outcome. Bootstrap confidence intervals refer to the raw intervention-minus-historical mean difference, not Hedges' g (p. 12, Section 3.5; p. 13, Table 2 note).

eligibility.reason: Not a randomized experiment: a historical-cohort comparison of two course offerings (pp. 9-10, Section 3.1), with GenAI bundled with a flipped-learning platform, so the contrast does not isolate AI. Only 28 people were analyzed (12 historical-control students and 16 intervention students; p. 9, Section 3.1; p. 13, Section 4.1), below 50. The output-scoring criterion is met: major deliverables were graded using analytic rubrics (p. 4, Introduction), and Fig. 6 explicitly links individual deliverables produced to scoring by a single rater using the same rubric for both cohorts (p. 9, panels C-D). Creativity thinking is one of the instructor-scored rubric dimensions (p. 10, Section 3.2 and Table 1; p. 11, Section 3.4, Course scores). The single-instructor measurement does not negate that the ratings concern produced work. Core eligibility remains no because criteria 1 and 2 are not met; the quasi_people design maps to observational context.

one_line_finding: In a historical-cohort comparison (12 vs 16 students), the cohort taught with a flipped-learning platform plus GenAI image ideation scored higher on the instructor's creativity-thinking rubric dimension, 84.38 vs 79.50 (diff 4.88, 95% CI [1.81, 8.02], Hedges' g = 1.09; p. 13, Table 2), with AI bundled with other course changes.
